clinicalPearls: The most common congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia; autosomal recessive, caused by biallelic SEC23B mutations affecting COPII endoplasmic-reticulum-to-Golgi trafficking.
Historically termed HEMPAS: hereditary erythroblastic multinuclearity with a positive acidified serum lysis test.
Bone marrow shows characteristic bi- and multinucleated erythroblasts, with a double plasma membrane appearance on electron microscopy.

The acidified-serum (Ham) test is positive with a proportion of ABO-compatible normal sera but negative with the patient's own serum, and the sucrose lysis test is negative, which distinguishes it from paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.
Red cell membrane SDS-PAGE shows hypoglycosylated, faster-migrating band 3 (anion exchanger 1).
Iron overload develops independently of transfusion because of ineffective erythropoiesis and suppressed hepcidin, so ferritin and organ iron should be monitored.
Splenectomy can raise the haemoglobin but does not correct iron loading, and pigment gallstones are common.
Anaemia is often mild to moderate, so the diagnosis is easily missed unless dyserythropoiesis is specifically sought.
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia type 2 is an autosomal recessive disorder of ineffective erythropoiesis caused by biallelic mutations in SEC23B, which encodes a core component of the COPII coat complex that mediates anterograde protein transport from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus. Impaired vesicular trafficking disrupts glycosylation of erythroid membrane proteins, producing the hallmark hypoglycosylated band 3 (anion exchanger 1) and abnormal N-linked glycans. Erythroblasts become bi- and multinucleated and undergo intramedullary apoptosis, so red cell production is ineffective despite marrow erythroid hyperplasia. Chronic haemolysis together with inappropriately low hepcidin increases dietary iron absorption, driving progressive parenchymal iron overload that can occur even in patients who have never been transfused.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital dyserythropoietic anaemias (types I and III, and CDA variants such as KLF1- or GATA1-related)
Hereditary spherocytosis and other red cell membrane disorders
additionalInvestigations: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to assess erythroblast morphology
Electron microscopy of erythroblasts for the double-membrane appearance
Acidified serum (Ham) and sucrose lysis tests, with flow cytometry (CD55/CD59) to exclude paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria
Red cell membrane protein SDS-PAGE for band 3 glycosylation
Iron studies and ferritin, with hepatic and cardiac iron quantification by MRI
Reticulocyte count, haptoglobin, bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase
redFlags: Symptomatic iron overload with cardiac, hepatic or endocrine dysfunction
Aplastic crisis, for example after parvovirus B19, with an abrupt fall in haemoglobin
Symptomatic gallstone disease or biliary obstruction
reference.prognosis: Many patients have mild-to-moderate anaemia and a near-normal life expectancy, but iron overload is the major long-term threat and can cause organ damage if not monitored and treated. Anaemia severity is variable and a minority require regular transfusion.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria because of a positive acidified-serum test, when the patient's own serum does not lyse the cells and PNH flow cytometry is normal.
Attributing iron overload solely to transfusion and under-treating it in non-transfused patients.
Overlooking dyserythropoietic anaemia when reticulocytes are inappropriately low for the degree of anaemia.
Confusing the picture with thalassaemia intermedia.
management: Iron chelation with deferasirox, deferiprone or desferrioxamine is the therapeutic mainstay, since parenchymal iron overload accrues even without transfusion because ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin
Give folic acid supplementation to meet the demands of chronically expanded but ineffective erythropoiesis
Reserve leucodepleted, phenotype-matched red-cell transfusion for symptomatic or severe anaemia to limit alloimmunisation
Consider splenectomy in transfusion-dependent or symptomatically anaemic patients to reduce haemolysis, with prior vaccination against encapsulated organisms and awareness of thrombotic risk
Monitor hepatic and cardiac iron burden with serial ferritin and MRI, and screen for pigment gallstones from chronic haemolysis
Offer genetic counselling and cascade family testing given autosomal recessive SEC23B inheritance
Refer to a specialist haematology centre and consider allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in severe transfusion-dependent childhood disease
